solution.description: Read 4 divided by 2 as bare symbols, with nothing standing behind the numerals. At this point the learner has an operation to carry out but no picture of what it means.

Give the same operation a concrete referent: 4 marbles shared equally between 2 children. Dealing them out one for each child empties the pile in two rounds, so each child holds 2, which is exactly what 4 divided by 2 was asking for.

examples.problem_statement: Calculate time elapsed between 9 a.m. and 11 a.m.

solution.description: Here the concrete referent is the clock. Elapsed time is the later hour minus the earlier one, so subtract 9 from 11 and read the answer 2 in hours rather than as a bare number.
The referent is the 24-hour clock, whose afternoon hours continue counting past 12 instead of restarting. So add 12 to the 8 of 8 p.m., giving 20.

common_mistakes: Reading the second answer as plain 2 instead of 2 hours; the referent is what supplies the unit.
Adding 12 to a morning time as well; the plus 12 rule only applies to times from 1 p.m. onward.

concept.technique_name: rebuilding facts from commutativity, associativity and distributivity

solution.description: Instead of retrieving 2 times 3 from a memorized table, rebuild it from the definition: multiplying by 2 means taking two copies of 3, so the product becomes 3 plus 3.
Carry out that single addition. 3 plus 3 is 6, so the product is 6 with no table lookup used.
Check the same count in a different representation: a group of three dots beside another group of three dots is one collection of six dots.
Check it once more on a number line. Starting at 0 and making two jumps of 3 units to the right lands first on 3 and then on 6, the same answer reached a third way.
Rebuild the fact from the distributive property instead. Split 3 into 2 plus 1, multiply the 2 by each part to get 4 and 2, and add those partial products back to 6.

examples.problem_statement: Solve 7 × 8 using conceptual mastery of arithmetic.

solution.description: Rebuild 7 times 8 rather than recalling it. Split one factor into a friendlier sum, multiply the other factor by each part, and add the two partial products; the parts recombine to 56.

examples.problem_statement: Simplify the algebraic expression (a × b) / (b × a).

solution.description: Commutativity says a times b and b times a are the same product, so numerator and denominator are identical. A nonzero quantity divided by itself is 1, with no expansion needed.
Three identical factors multiplied together are written in exponent form: the repeated factor a with the count 3 raised above it, giving a cubed.

examples.problem_statement: Determine if the equation d/c + a = (d + a) / (c + a) is true.

solution.description: Test the claim rather than trusting its shape. Adding a to d over c changes only the numerator, while the right side also alters the denominator, so the two sides are not equal expressions and the statement is false.

key_reminders: {'point': "The text emphasizes the distinction between 'rote verbal knowledge' (e.g., multiplication tables, nursery rhymes) and 'conceptual mastery' or 'abstract formal calculations'."}
{'point': "It highlights that 'judiciously making use of the commutativity, associativity, and distributivity of arithmetic operations' allows for problem-solving even when rote memory fails."}
{'point': "It posits that algebraic knowledge may be 'largely independent of the networks involved in mental calculation'."}
common_mistakes: Assuming the right-hand form is legal because it looks tidy; adding a to the numerator and the denominator of d over c changes the value, so the identity is false.
Writing a times a times a as 3a instead of a cubed; the count 3 is how many factors there are, not a multiplier.
Splitting one factor for the distributive step and then forgetting to add the second partial product, which leaves 7 times 8 short of 56.

concept.technique_name: two-digit by one-digit multiplication, then difference

examples.problem_statement: A patient with prefrontal cortex damage is attempting to multiply 23 by 4. Due to their condition, they make the following errors: they add instead of multiply, process digits in the wrong order, forget to carry over, and mix up intermediate results. If they perform the calculation as 20 + 3 = 23, then 23 + 4 = 27, what is the difference between their incorrect result and the correct answer?

solution.description: Strip the scenario down to the arithmetic actually asked for: the correct product is 23 multiplied by 4.
Work that product out. Four twenties are 80 and four threes are 12, and 80 plus 12 is 92, so the correct answer is 92.

solution.operation: Identify the patient's incorrect calculation: $20 + 3 = 23$, then $23 + 4 = 27$
solution.description: Now trace what the patient did instead. They split 23 into 20 and 3 and added the parts back to 23, then added the 4 rather than multiplying by it, landing on 27.
The question asks how far apart the two results are, so subtract the patient's 27 from the correct 92, which leaves a gap of 65.

key_reminders: {'point': "The text highlights that mathematical success requires more than just calculation skills; it requires 'planning and verification'—functions of the 'central executive'."}
{'point': "It warns that without these, one might 'impulsively rush to the first calculation that jumps to mind' or 'fall prey to some repetitive response pattern'."}
{'point': "It also introduces the concept of 'cognitive estimation' as the ability to evaluate the 'plausibility of the retrieved result'."}
common_mistakes: Answering 92 or 27; the question asks for the gap between them, not either result on its own.
Repeating the patient's error and adding 4 to 23 instead of multiplying, which gives 27 rather than 92.
Losing the carry: four threes are 12, so the tens digit rises from 8 to 9 and the product is 92, not 82.
repair_note: All four descriptions were empty and have been written; each now narrates its own operation, including the actual carry work behind 23 times 4 equal to 92 and why step 4 subtracts. Corrected technique_name from the placeholder 'N/A' to the operation the steps perform. Scaffold arrow_matrix replaced with textual_scaffold, since the steps set out the two results in prose and build no diagram. Added three hazards specific to 23 times 4 and to the difference the question asks for.

concept.technique_name: constructing a nonstandard model of the Peano axioms

examples.problem_statement: Construct a simplified metaphor for a nonstandard model of arithmetic (Set A).

solution.description: Begin from the familiar ground: the standard natural numbers 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on. The nonstandard model will be this set with extra elements bolted on, so it has to be named first.
Add a single new element, written omega, and declare it larger than every natural number. That one declaration is what makes the model nonstandard, because no natural number can play that role.

Arithmetic requires every element to have a successor, so omega alone is not enough. Add omega plus 1, omega plus 2 and so on, one new element for each natural number n, all distinct from each other and from the naturals.
Take the union of the two collections built so far, the standard naturals and the whole omega block, and call it A. That union is the nonstandard model being constructed.

Finally check the construction against the axioms. A must satisfy the same first-order properties as the standard model, and the interesting failure point is induction, since the omega block is never reached by counting up from 0.

examples.answer: A = {0, 1, 2, 3, ..., ω, ω+1, ω+2, ...} (with ω being an infinite element)

key_reminders: {'point': "The text uses a 'simplified metaphor' to explain a complex logical concept."}
common_mistakes: Treating omega as merely a very large natural number; it is defined to exceed every natural number, so it lies outside the standard set entirely.
Adding omega on its own and stopping there, which leaves elements without successors and breaks the arithmetic the model is supposed to satisfy.
Expecting to reach omega by counting 0, 1, 2 and onward; nothing in the omega block is a finite number of successor steps from 0, which is exactly why induction is the axiom at risk.
repair_note: Rewrote all five descriptions. Three ended in stranded sentence fragments left behind when symbols were stripped out ('Let be a new element such that for all', 'For each , define as distinct elements', 'Check that satisfies all axioms'), and one carried LaTeX math-mode delimiters around omega. Each now reads as prose about its own operation and result. Sharpened technique_name from 'Peano axioms' to the construction the steps actually carry out. Scaffold place_value_chart replaced with textual_scaffold: no place values appear anywhere, the steps define and union sets in words and symbols. Added three hazards; the template previously had no common_mistakes field.

examples.problem_statement: In an experiment on the SNARC effect, participants are shown numbers at the center of a screen, followed by a dot appearing either to the left or right. The time to detect the dot is influenced by the number's magnitude. Suppose a participant is shown the number 8, and the dot appears 200 ms later. If the dot appears on the right, detection time is 50 ms faster than baseline. If the dot appears on the left, detection time is 50 ms slower than baseline. What is the difference in detection time between left and right dots when the number 8 is shown?

solution.operation: When the dot appears on the right with a large number (8), detection time is 50 ms faster than baseline
solution.description: Take the right-hand case first. With the large number 8 on screen, a dot on the right is detected 50 ms faster than baseline, so its time is baseline minus 50.

solution.operation: When the dot appears on the left with a large number (8), detection time is 50 ms slower than baseline
solution.description: Now the left-hand case, same number. A dot on the left is detected 50 ms slower than baseline, so its time is baseline plus 50.

solution.operation: The difference in detection time between left and right = (baseline + 50) - (baseline - 50) = 100 ms
solution.description: Subtract the two to get the gap. The unknown baseline cancels, leaving 50 plus 50, so left and right differ by 100 ms.
Subtract 21 from 32 directly: 2 units take away 1 unit leaves 1, and 3 tens take away 2 tens leaves 1 ten, so the difference is 11 with no borrowing needed.

key_reminders: {'point': "The text introduces the 'neuronal recycling principle' as a core conceptual framework."}
common_mistakes: Answering 50 ms, which is how far each side shifts from baseline; the question asks for the gap between the two sides, which is twice that.
Trying to find the baseline first; it cancels in the subtraction and is never needed.
Subtracting in the wrong order, as 21 minus 32, and reporting a negative count of candies.

Example 2 carried the clearest misattachment in this template: a step whose operation is 'Subtraction' on 32 minus 21 was described as 'moving right 21 units from 32 gives the sum of 53', which narrates an addition on a number line from a different example; it was replaced with the actual subtraction. examples.problem_statement: Infant cracker choice experiment (Lisa Feigenson): Determine the limits of an infant's ability to choose the larger of two hidden quantities.

solution.description: Fix the threshold everything else will be measured against. Infants track small collections exactly, but only up to about three or four items at once.
Test 2 against 3. Both sit at or below the limit, so the infant can hold each collection exactly and pick the larger one, and this is the case where infants succeed.
Test 2 against 4. The 2 is fine, but 4 is past the limit and cannot be represented exactly, so there is nothing precise to compare the 2 with and the choice fails.
Test 1 against 4. The same thing happens even though 1 is very small: it is the 4 on the other side that breaks the comparison, not the size of the gap.
Test 3 against 6. The 3 is right at the limit and the 6 is well beyond it, so the comparison fails again despite the two-to-one ratio that would seem to make it easy.

Read the pattern off the four cases: success whenever both quantities stay within about three, failure as soon as either one exceeds it. The limit, not the difference between the numbers, is what predicts the outcome.

examples.answer: Infants succeed on 2 vs 3 but fail on 2 vs 4, 1 vs 4, and 3 vs 6 when one number exceeds the object-tracking limit.

key_reminders: {'point': 'The text employs narrative evidence to explain abstract cognitive concepts.'}
{'point': "It uses rhetorical questions ('Why does the infant succeed on 2 versus 3, and fail with 2 versus 4...?') to prompt critical thinking."}
{'point': "Key pedagogical signals include: 'Surprisingly, however...', 'Indeed, some of the best evidence...', 'Consider, for instance...', and 'Unsurprisingly...'."}
{'point': 'Footnotes 51, 52, and 53 serve as academic anchors for the claims made.'}
common_mistakes: Predicting success on 2 versus 4 because the gap is wider than in 2 versus 3; what decides the outcome is whether either quantity passes the tracking limit.
Reading 3 versus 6 as an easy double; the 6 cannot be tracked exactly, so the ratio never comes into play.
repair_note: Rewrote all six descriptions. Four ended in orphaned connector words left over from stripped symbols ('items', 'and both', 'but'), and none explained why the comparison fails rather than merely restating that it does. Corrected technique_name from the broad 'cognitive development' to the object-tracking limit, which is the single rule every step applies. Kept visual_scaffold as textual_scaffold: each step compares a quantity against a threshold in words, with no diagram built. Added two hazards drawn from the specific pairs tested here.

examples.problem_statement: Sarah has 21 candies. She gets 30 more. John has 34 candies. Who has more?

solution.description: Pin down the starting quantity given in the problem: Sarah has 21 candies before anything is added.
She then receives 30 more, so her total is that starting 21 with 30 added to it. Set the addition up before evaluating it.
Add the tens and the units separately: 30 brings three more tens to the 2 tens in 21, and the single unit is untouched, giving 51.
John's count needs no work, since nothing is added to or taken from it. He has 34.
Compare the two totals now that both are known. 51 is greater than 34, so Sarah ends up with more candies.

key_reminders: {'point': 'The trick, as seen in Figure 10.8, is that the test only requires an approximate understanding of quantities.'}
{'point': 'Their answers are only statistically correct (about 70% of the time), but they improve as the distance between the two choices increases.'}
{'point': 'Furthermore, they are worse with subtraction than with addition, exactly as predicted by a mathematical theory of the approximation process.'}
{'point': 'Success in this approximation test was a good predictor of the children’s later scores in mathematics.'}
common_mistakes: Comparing Sarah's opening 21 with John's 34 and answering John, before adding the 30 she receives.
Adding the 30 to John's total as well; only Sarah is given more candies.
repair_note: Descriptions merely echoed their operation labels ('Sarah starts with 21 candies', 'John has 34 candies') without saying what the step does or why it follows; each was rewritten to carry its own arithmetic and its role in the comparison. Corrected technique_name from 'approximation' to add-then-compare: nothing in the steps is approximated, 21 plus 30 is computed exactly as 51 and then compared. Scaffold place_value_chart replaced with equation_chain, since the steps run a chain of equalities into a final inequality rather than filling a place-value grid. Added two hazards about the order of operations in this word problem.

examples.problem_statement: A chimpanzee is presented with two trays. Tray 1 has piles of 4 and 3 chocolate chips. Tray 2 has piles of 5 and 1 chocolate chips. Which tray will the chimpanzee choose to maximize its reward?

solution.description: Read the first tray as a sum rather than as two separate heaps: it holds a pile of 4 chips and a pile of 3, so its value is 4 plus 3.
Evaluate that sum. 4 and 3 make 7, the total the first tray is worth.
Do the same for the second tray, which holds a pile of 5 and a pile of 1, so its value is 5 plus 1.
Evaluate the second sum. 5 and 1 make 6, the total the second tray is worth.
Now compare the two totals rather than the individual piles. 7 is greater than 6, so the first tray carries more chips overall.
An animal maximizing reward takes the larger total, so the choice falls on the first tray with its 7 chips.

examples.answer: The chimpanzee selects the first tray (total of 7).

key_reminders: {'point': 'The text uses a narrative case study to demonstrate a multi-step logical process.'}
common_mistakes: Choosing the second tray because its biggest single pile, 5, beats the biggest pile on the first tray; what counts is the total of both piles.
Comparing the small piles, 3 against 1, instead of adding each tray up first.
repair_note: Descriptions were close to correct but restated the operation labels; each was rewritten to say what the step does with its own numbers and why it comes next, and the closing step now states the maximizing rule rather than repeating the comparison. technique_name 'addition' matches what the steps do and was kept. Scaffold place_value_chart replaced with equation_chain: all four quantities are single digits, no place values are decomposed, and the steps form a chain of sums ending in an inequality. Added two hazards about comparing piles instead of totals.

concept.technique_name: scaling a range by a constant count

examples.problem_statement: Robinson uses a water accumulator to count cannibals arriving at his island. Each time a cannibal lands, he diverts a fixed amount of water into the accumulator. The water flow varies randomly between 4 and 6 liters per second, and each diversion lasts exactly 1 second. If Robinson counts 10 cannibals arriving, what is the possible range of total water (in liters) in the accumulator after counting all cannibals?

solution.operation: Minimum volume per diversion = 4 L/s × 1 s = 4 L.
solution.description: Take the slowest case first. At the low end of the flow range, 4 liters per second running for the 1 second a diversion lasts puts 4 liters into the accumulator.

solution.operation: Maximum volume per diversion = 6 L/s × 1 s = 6 L.
solution.description: Take the fastest case the same way. 6 liters per second for 1 second puts 6 liters in, so a single diversion is worth somewhere between 4 and 6 liters.

solution.operation: For 10 diversions, total minimum volume = 10 × 4 = 40 L.
solution.description: Ten cannibals mean ten diversions. If every one of them ran at the slow end, the accumulator would hold 10 times 4, that is 40 liters, the smallest total possible.
If instead every diversion ran at the fast end, the total would be 10 times 6, that is 60 liters, the largest total possible.

solution.operation: Thus the water volume is between 40 and 60 liters.
solution.description: Since no run can fall below the all-slow total or rise above the all-fast one, the accumulator ends up holding between 40 and 60 liters.

solution.operation: 1. Minimum water per cannibal = minimum flow rate × time = 4 L/s × 1 s = 4 L
solution.description: The same derivation is now set out again as a numbered check. Restate the per-cannibal minimum as flow rate times duration, 4 liters per second for 1 second, giving 4 liters.

solution.operation: 2. Maximum water per cannibal = maximum flow rate × time = 6 L/s × 1 s = 6 L
solution.description: Restate the per-cannibal maximum the same way, 6 liters per second for 1 second, giving 6 liters.

solution.operation: 3. For 10 cannibals, minimum total water = 10 × 4 L = 40 L
solution.description: Scale the minimum up to the full count: 10 cannibals at 4 liters each is 40 liters, matching the lower bound found earlier.

solution.operation: 4. For 10 cannibals, maximum total water = 10 × 6 L = 60 L
solution.description: Scale the maximum up to the full count: 10 cannibals at 6 liters each is 60 liters, matching the upper bound found earlier.

solution.operation: 5. Therefore, the total water in the accumulator will be between 40 and 60 liters
solution.description: Both routes agree, so the total water in the accumulator lies between 40 and 60 liters.

solution.operation: Identify the minimum value of the water flow rate from the given parameters: 4 liters per second.
solution.description: Return to the givens once more and read off the low end of the stated flow range, 4 liters per second, the number every minimum in this problem is built from.

solution.operation: Identify the maximum value of the water flow rate from the given parameters: 6 liters per second.
solution.description: Read off the high end of the same stated range, 6 liters per second, the number behind every maximum above.

solution.operation: The range of the water flow rate is from 4 to 6 liters per second.
solution.description: Put the two endpoints together: the flow rate itself spans 4 to 6 liters per second, and it is this 2-liter-per-second spread, multiplied by the 10 diversions, that opens the final answer into a 20-liter window.

key_reminders: {'point': 'This is the distance effect.'}
{'point': 'This effect will be exacerbated as the numbers become larger, thus reproducing the magnitude effect that also characterizes animal behavior.'}
{'point': 'The accumulator metaphor thus helps us to understand why rat behavior is so variable from one trial to the next.'}
{'point': 'To a rat, numbers are just approximate magnitudes, variable from one time to time, and as fleeting and elusive as the duration of sounds or the saturation of colors.'}
common_mistakes: Multiplying only the middle of the range, 5 liters, and reporting a single total of 50 instead of a range.
Multiplying the flow rate by 10 seconds; each diversion lasts 1 second, and it is the number of cannibals that is 10.
Giving the answer as 40 to 60 but forgetting that both endpoints are attainable only if every one of the ten diversions happens to run at the same extreme.

concept.technique_name: Piagetian tests of number logic: conservation and class inclusion

examples.problem_statement: The 'number conservation' test: Children are shown two equally spaced rows of six glasses and six bottles. Then, one row (the glasses) is spread out to be longer than the other.

solution.description: Lay out the apparatus before anything is changed: a row of 6 glasses directly above a row of 6 bottles, with the items equally spaced so the two rows are the same length.
Establish the starting fact the test depends on. Counting each row gives 6 and 6, so the child agrees the two quantities are equal before any transformation.
Change only the spacing: pull the glasses apart so their row stretches past the bottles. No glass is added and none removed, so the count is untouched and only the length has altered.
Watch what the child attends to. The stretched row is visibly longer, and the child treats longer as meaning more, reading a difference in length as a difference in number.
Compare that judgment against the fact from step 2. The rows still hold 6 and 6, yet the child now says the glasses are more numerous, so number has not been conserved across the change.

solution.result: \text{Conservation of number} \notin \text{Preoperational stage} \\ \text{Conservation of number} \in \text{Concrete operational stage}
solution.description: Place the failure in Piaget's scheme: judging by appearance is what marks the preoperational stage, and the ability to hold number fixed across such a transformation arrives with the concrete operational stage.

examples.answer: Children fail to 'conserve number' and judge quantity by length.

examples.problem_statement: The class inclusion test: A child is shown a bunch of eight flowers consisting of six roses and two tulips. Question: 'Are there more roses or more flowers?'

solution.description: Sort the bunch into the sets the question names. There are 6 roses and 2 tulips, and the roses are a part of the 8 flowers rather than a rival group beside them.

Now make the comparison the question asks for, roses against flowers, that is 6 against 8. A part can never outnumber the whole that contains it, so there are more flowers, yet most children compare the roses with the tulips instead and answer that the roses are more numerous.

examples.answer: Most children will say 'the roses are more numerous than the flowers'.

key_reminders: {'point': "Key concepts: 'number conservation' test."}
{'point': "Educational impact: 'precocious teaching of mathematics is a vain or even harmful enterprise' according to Piagetian theory."}
common_mistakes: Believing the spread-out row really does gain glasses; moving items apart changes the length of the row, not how many things are in it.
Answering that there are more roses than flowers; the 6 roses are counted inside the 8 flowers, so the comparison is 6 against 8, not 6 against the 2 tulips.
repair_note: Example 2's two descriptions belonged to example 1: a class-inclusion step was described as comparing quantities 'after transformation to reinforce conservation' and as confirming that 'quantity remains constant despite visual changes', which is the conservation example's work. Both were rewritten to narrate the roses-and-flowers sets and the part-whole comparison, and example 1's six descriptions were expanded from label echoes into narration of their own operations. Corrected technique_name from 'number conservation', which covers only the first example, to the pair of Piagetian tests the template actually contains. Kept visual_scaffold as textual_scaffold, since the rows are described rather than constructed on any of the available structures. Added two hazards, one per example.
